To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) adolescents with GD treated with GnRHA showed sex-atypical activation in brain regions that have been associated with ToL performance in control groups, but did not show sex-atypical performance, and (2), GnRHa did not alter the sex-atypical activation of the brain regions that have previously been associated with To L performance in adolescents with gender-dysphoria.
1) GnRHA treatment had no effect of ToL performance in GD adolescents, and 2) pubertial hormones may induce sex atypical brain activation during EF in GD adolescents.
GnRHa treatment of adolescents with GD had no effect on EF performance and that untreated adolescents with GD show sex-atypical brain activation during EF.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of GnRHa treatment on EF and the neural underpinnings of sex differences in EF in adolescents with gender identity disorder.
the question whether puberty suppression affects executive functions in adolescents with gender identity disorder (GID).
the effect of GnRha treatment on executive function in adolescents with GD and the neural correlates of this treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of puberty suppression treatment in GD adolescents on executive functions is not clear.
GnRHa treatment does not alter ToL performance in MFs and FMs and that the sex differences in ToL activation are not altered in GnRHa-treated adolescents with GD.
GnRHa treatment in adolescents with GD does not alter EF and does not affect the sexual dimorphism in EF-related brain activation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

adolescents with gender dysmorphia (GD) who are treated with puberty suppressants (GnRHA) have brain activations during executive functioning tasks that are similar to the sex of their natal sex (the sex assigned at birth), and not the sex they identify with.
the suppression of puberty in adolescents with GD may not have any effect on EF performance, while the development of puberty might induce sex-atypical neural activation during EF.
adolescents with GD treated with GnRha show similar sex-differences in brain activations during the ToL as their natal sex peers, but show less activation in the right prefrontal cortex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
adolescents with GD treated with GnRHas have sex-atypical activation patterns in the DLPFC and precuneus during EF.
GnRHa treatment did not affect ToL performance in our adolescents with GD.
adolescents with GD may be at risk to show sex-atypical brain activation during EF and that GnRHa treatment does not alter this risk.
